text.p: LIFFE robusta coffee futures stayed lower into Friday midday close on follow-through trade selling after a sell-off in New York on Thursday but persistent roaster buying at the lows helped slow the decline.
There was no fresh news but traders said easing concerns over Brazilian frost and a build in New York exchange-certified stocks were the main underlying bearish factors.

"It's all coming to an end, slowly but surely," said one trader. The market had seen an unprecedented five-month rally that peaked in late May on aggressive fund and roaster buying, tight arabica supplies and frost fears in Brazil.

June and July are the frost-danger months in Brazil but so far there has been no crop-damaging freeze in the country's coffee-growing areas. Chances of a frost in the coming weeks are also slim, according to weathermen.
By the midday pause, most-active September stood $25 down at $1,746 per tonne after hitting the session's floor at $1,745. Its intraday high was $1,758.
It earlier made a due of $20 down.
On the charts, coffee faces a major support at $1,695, the lower end of the June trading range. A break lower could see a swift move down to $1,600.
On the upside, a breakthrough at above $1,850 would pave the way for the market to regain a foothold at $2,040, a level last seen in May.
In its commentary on Friday, broker GNI said the odds of a frost from hereon were around 20:1, rising to 63:1 by the end of the month and 100:1 just five days after that.
"Clearly the frost premium should be eroding rapidly, and the current warm conditions are allowing this year's harvest to continue apace," it said.
